questions.q: What problem does feature versioning solve that a feature's name alone cannot?
options: It makes feature computation run faster
It distinguishes between different versions of a feature's logic over time, even when the name stays the same, so a silent change doesn't create ambiguity
It eliminates the need for an online store
It automatically fixes training/serving skew without any code changes
questions.explain: Without versioning, a silent change to a FeatureView's logic means models trained before and after the change both appear to use the same named feature, even though their behavior differs — versioning tracks exactly which logic was in effect when.

questions.q: What does the `feast apply` command do?
options: Trains a new model using the current feature definitions
Pushes feature and entity definition changes from source control into the live registry
Deletes all historical data from the offline store
Switches the online store backend from Redis to DynamoDB
questions.explain: feast apply syncs the live registry to match what's currently defined in source control, ensuring the registry never diverges from a tracked, committed definition.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three lineage questions described in this lesson?
options: How much does the feature store cost per month
Which model versions were trained using a specific feature definition, and which are still using an older one
What color scheme does the Feast UI use
How many GPUs are available in the training cluster
questions.explain: One of the three lineage questions is feature-to-model: tracing which model versions were trained against a specific feature definition versus an older one.

questions.q: Why is lineage described as 'the forward-looking twin of training/serving skew detection'?
options: Because both require deleting the offline store
Because skew detection compares two live numbers now, while lineage reconstructs history after the fact to explain what happened
Because lineage and skew detection are the exact same process with different names
Because lineage only applies to online stores, and skew only applies to offline stores
questions.explain: Skew detection compares current serving and offline values directly; lineage instead answers historical questions after an incident or audit — what definition and data produced a specific past prediction.

questions.q: Why does feature versioning and lineage matter especially in regulated industries like finance or healthcare?
options: Regulations require all models to use open-source feature stores
Auditors often require a company to show exactly which data and logic produced a specific past decision, not just the decision itself
Regulated industries are not allowed to use online stores
Lineage is only relevant to unregulated startups
questions.explain: In regulated industries, auditors commonly require traceability from a past decision back to the exact feature definitions and data used — which is exactly what versioning and lineage provide.
